messages.author: 5ff906c2720491d5
messages.subject: age-structured CJS model in nimble
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am pretty new to Nimble with some experience with JAGS (and jagsUI package).
I want to calculate WAIC to do model selection on different age-structured CJS models. That is why I decided to convert my JAGS codes to Nimble.
The code is adapted from Kery and Schaub's Bayesian Population Analysis Using WinBUGS book, section 7.7. 

For my global (most complex model) I am trying to calculate survival and recapture rates for 2-age levels (Juvenile and Adult), 2-sexes (Female and Male), and 2-seasons (Dry and Wet). Recapture probability function also has random year effect.
I calculate the desired derived parameters inside the model. (see attached code global_x.R and some data to run it data_x.R)

It looks like model runs smoothly, however since I want to get WAIC, I am also monitoring the p and z values of the likelihood in my parameters of interest, and when I try to check diagnostics of z (sometimes p too with other models not the global one) with MCMCsummary or MCMCtrace functions like so

MCMCsummary(out_p1global$samples, params = "z", round=3)
MCMCtrace(out_p1global$samples, params = "z", pdf=F, ind = T, Rhat = T, n.eff = T)

it gives me an error as: 
"Error in quantile.default(newX[, i], ...) : 
  missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE"

I tried to look what is wrong by checking the values of z in the first chain as:
temp.z <- out_p1global$samples[[1]][,grep("z", colnames(out_p1global$samples[[1]]))]
and it looks like the first row has NAs. I have NAs in the age matrix covariate (agemat) until the first capture (logically), I have NAs in the initial values of until the next time step of the first capture (again logically). Finally, I have NAs in the initial values of slopes wherever I fixed them to a value in the model.

I try all my models first with these MCMC settings
ni <- 10; nt <- 1 ; nb <- 5 ; nc <- 3 .

So, to solve the issue I tried:
1. same model without asking for WAIC, got the same error.
2. Run the same model with WAIC with better MCMC settings and longer iterations
na <- 5000 ; ni <- 150000; nt <- 20 ; nb <-5000 ; nc <- 3, got the same error.

I also ran the same model with same MCMC settings in JAGS as well and the estimates from JAGS and Nimble were same, so I'm guessing this might not be a coding error in the model?

My questions are
  1. Any idea how to solve this issue?
  2. Only reason I am monitoring p and z is WAIC. Can I trust the calculated WAIC?
  3. Again, since I don't need the estimates of p and z anyway, does this issue matter for the rest of my parameter estimates if their diagnostics are fine? Can I still use estimates to calculate predictions even if I get this error for z and p (sometimes both of them depending on the model)?
Thank you for all the help in advance, sorry for rather long message.
Best,
Dilsad

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: age-structured CJS model in nimble
parts:
hi Dilsad,

Sorry about the late reply - this one "fell through the cracks".

A few thoughts here:

1) WAIC uses the likelihood at each iteration (since v. 0.12.0, if using the new "online" WAIC we offer) or the likelihood at each monitored sample (in earlier versions). Since the likelihood for 'y' depends on 'p' and 'z', the key thing is that the likelihood not be NA. When I run your code, I see that the likelihood can be calculated once the initial values are set even though there are some NA values for some elements of 'z'. So I think the WAIC calculation should be fine.

2) If you have some elements of z that are deterministic and not used, then I don't think it makes sense to try and summarize their posterior samples as you are doing. I would only check the MCMC mixing of the z's that are stochastic and being sampled. 

The p's are deterministic. For those that are not fixed to be constant values, but instead depend on other parameters that are being sampled, it's fine to check their mixing if you want to.

3) Since the z and p values that are given NA are not ever used, you could probably just set them to 0 without any ill effects and then you wouldn't see the warnings about NAs when you use the MCMCvis  package functions on the monitored values of all the z's and all the p's, which includes those that are not being sampled and for which the diagnostics are not meaningful.

I might not have fully followed what the issue is, so feel free to follow up.

-chris

parts:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for the really elaborated reply, it helped me to understand what the issue is a lot.

I really do not think it is that important that I check the diagnostics of p and z anyway, because I do not use them for predictions etc. I monitor them only so that nimble can calculate WAIC. I am checking the traceplots of all the alphas and betas in the model to check the model diagnostics and then use the derived parameters for the main predictions from the model. I think based on what you are saying there is nothing wrong with doing this? And if all convergence issues are fine I can also trust WAIC for model selection right?

Also, another issue is, models are actually not converging even with iterations more that 300k. I check traceplots of all alphas and betas, because I think these are the ones that needs to be good, and they look really bad. I also check Rhat, depending on the model it might be fine sometimes but still I trust traceplots more. I tried to change priors and come up with a solution, however so far I did not have any luck. When you ran the model, did you see anything weird or illogical that might cause that?

Thanks.
Best,
Dilsad

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: age-structured CJS model in nimble
parts:
That's correct, I don't see any problems with using NIMBLE's WAIC here. Also note with the current version of nimble, you don't need to monitor any particular nodes. We now have an 'online' WAIC calculation that doesn't require monitors, so in fact you don't need to monitor p and z if you are not interested in them. 

As far as convergence, that's a big question, and I didn't look in detail at your model from that perspective. Perhaps others on the list might have suggestions for these types of models. Trying different types of samplers, blocking parameters, reparameterizing, etc. could all be possibilities.
But you might first want to look at our nimbleEcology package, which provides a Cormack-Jolly-Seber model structure that might be helpful because it analytically integrates over the latent states so that the MCMC doesn't have to sample them. This has the potential to speed up the MCMC on a per-iteration basis and improve mixing by reducing the dimension of the parameter space and potentially reducing posterior correlation.

-chris
